before.content_html:
What Was Apartheid?

Apartheid was the system of rigid racial segregation enforced by South Africa's National Party (NP) government after its election victory in 1948. The NP argued that separate racial “nations” should develop independently — a policy its architects called Separate Development. In practice, it meant a white minority of around 20 per cent of the population controlled the land, wealth and government, while black South Africans were stripped of citizenship rights.

The system rested on a battery of laws. The Population Registration Act (1950) classified every person at birth into one of four racial categories: White, Coloured, Indian or Native (later Bantu). This classification determined where you could live, work, go to school and whom you could marry.

Key Fact

The Population Registration Act (1950), Group Areas Act (1950) and Bantu Education Act (1953) formed the legal spine of apartheid, controlling where people lived, what work they could do, and what education they could access.

Key Laws of Apartheid

The Group Areas Act (1950) designated separate residential zones by race. Black and Coloured families who lived in areas reclassified as “white” were forcibly removed — an estimated 3.5 million people were displaced between 1960 and 1983. The pass book (later the reference book) tied black workers to particular employers and geographical areas. Failure to carry it could mean immediate arrest.

The Bantu Education Act (1953) placed African schooling under government control and introduced an inferior curriculum. The system's chief architect, Hendrik Verwoerd, was explicit: he argued that black Africans should not be educated “above the level of certain forms of labour”. Funding per pupil in African schools was a fraction of the amount spent on white pupils.

Verwoerd's Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act (1959) created ten Bantustans (homelands), each theoretically a future “self-governing” nation for a particular ethnic group. In reality the homelands covered just 13 per cent of South Africa's land — mostly the poorest, least fertile areas. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act (1970) stripped black South Africans of their South African citizenship and reassigned it to their designated homeland, even if they had never lived there.

The Transkei (1963) was the first homeland to be granted nominal “self-government”, led by Kaiser Matanzima. No foreign government recognised any homeland as genuinely independent. The policy allowed the apartheid government to claim it was not oppressing South African citizens — because in its legal framework, black residents were now citizens of foreign territories.

Support and Opposition Within White Society

The apartheid regime did not enjoy unanimous white support. The mainly English-speaking United Party opposed some aspects of the system, and a small number of Afrikaners, including the Broederbond-linked theologian Beyers Naude, broke with the Dutch Reformed Church's endorsement of segregation. However, elections were restricted to whites, and the NP won successive majorities, particularly after the 1961 republic referendum which ended South Africa's Commonwealth membership.

Key Fact

The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act (1970) stripped millions of black South Africans of their South African citizenship, reclassifying them as citizens of their designated homeland — a legal fiction designed to justify denying them political rights in South Africa itself.

Historians distinguish between “petty apartheid” (segregation of everyday public spaces — separate park benches, beaches, entrances, toilets and bus stops) and “grand apartheid” (the structural laws denying political rights and enforcing geographical separation). Both operated simultaneously. Petty apartheid was the system's most visible face; grand apartheid was its deepest damage.

The Economic Logic of Apartheid

White-owned mines, farms and industries depended on an abundant supply of cheap, controlled African labour. Pass laws ensured that black workers could be directed to where employers needed them and expelled from cities when they were not. Historian Saul Dubow has argued that apartheid was not simply ideological racism but a system with clear economic beneficiaries among white employers and workers who were protected from black competition in skilled trades.

Racial Classification in Practice

The Population Registration Act created categories that were applied inconsistently and with damaging consequences for families. People of mixed heritage were sometimes classified differently from their siblings. Appeals were possible but rare and humiliating. The classification determined not just where someone could live, but also which schools their children could attend, which hospitals they could use and whether interracial marriage was legal under the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949) and the Immorality Amendment Act (1950). These laws were applied in courts and could lead to criminal prosecution.

The Suppression of Communism Act (1950) gave the government broad powers to ban individuals and organisations it defined as “communist” — a definition that extended far beyond members of the Communist Party to include anyone who advocated racial equality or opposed the government. This Act was used extensively against the ANC, trade unionists and white liberals throughout the apartheid period, effectively making opposition to racism a criminal offence.

The Dutch Reformed Church and Ideological Justification

The Dutch Reformed Church played a significant role in providing theological justification for apartheid, claiming that the separation of races was sanctioned by the Bible. This gave many Afrikaners a moral framework for the system that went beyond mere self-interest. By the 1980s, however, a growing number of Dutch Reformed ministers were challenging this position, and in 1990 the Church formally declared that apartheid had been a sin.

lessons.title: Sharpeville and the turn to armed struggle

before.content_html:
The Road to Sharpeville

By 1960, the African National Congress had spent almost half a century campaigning against racial laws through non-violent protest: petitions, strikes and civil disobedience. The Freedom Charter, adopted at Kliptown on 26 June 1955, set out a vision of a multiracial democratic South Africa. It remained the ANC's foundational document throughout the struggle.

In 1959 a breakaway group, the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), formed under Robert Sobukwe. The PAC rejected white allies and called for an Africa-first approach, targeting the pass laws as the single most hated symbol of apartheid.

Key Fact

On 21 March 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of approximately 5,000 unarmed protesters at Sharpeville township near Vereeniging. Sixty-nine people were killed and around 180 wounded. Most of those killed were shot in the back as they fled. Hospital records analysed in 2023 suggest the real toll may have been higher — at least 91 dead and 281 wounded — with police likely under-reporting by roughly a third.

The Sharpeville Massacre

The PAC had organised a national campaign against pass laws on 21 March 1960, calling on Africans to leave their passes at home and present themselves at police stations for arrest. At Sharpeville, a crowd of around 5,000 gathered at the local police station. The exact sequence of events before the shooting is disputed; the police opened fire and continued shooting even as the crowd fled. Sixty-nine people died; the majority were shot in the back.

The images of the dead — widely circulated internationally — caused worldwide outrage. ANC president-general Albert Luthuli publicly burned his own pass card in protest. In response, the government declared a state of emergency and, on 8 April 1960, banned both the ANC and the PAC under the Unlawful Organisations Act.

Banned and driven underground, the ANC leadership debated its response to Sharpeville. A significant faction, including Nelson Mandela, concluded that half a century of peaceful protest had achieved nothing and that a new strategy was required. In December 1961, Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK, “Spear of the Nation”) was launched as the ANC’s military wing.

MK’s initial strategy was sabotage of infrastructure — power lines, government buildings and transport links — not attacks on people. Mandela and the ANC leadership made a deliberate decision to avoid killing civilians. This is important for historical accuracy: the apartheid government labelled MK as terrorists, but its founding strategy was deliberately aimed at property, not people. MK’s strategy would evolve over the following decades.

Poqo and the PAC’s Armed Response

Poqo (“Pure” or “Alone” in Xhosa) emerged as the PAC’s armed wing around 1961–62. Unlike MK’s sabotage focus, Poqo carried out attacks that included killing informers and, in some instances, white civilians. This distinction between MK’s initial strategy and Poqo’s approach is significant for understanding the range of responses within the anti-apartheid movement.

Key Fact

The immediate impact of Sharpeville: the government declared a state of emergency, banned the ANC and PAC (April 1960) and arrested thousands of activists. The long-term consequence was that both organisations were driven underground and turned to armed struggle.

Oliver Tambo slipped out of South Africa in 1960 before the banning orders took effect. He spent the next thirty years leading the ANC’s external mission from Lusaka, Zambia, building international support, running MK training camps in Angola and Tanzania, and lobbying foreign governments and the United Nations. Without Tambo’s work in exile, the ANC might have collapsed as an organisation during the “long silence” of the 1960s and 1970s.

The ANC and the Freedom Charter — Continued Relevance

Despite the banning of the ANC, the Freedom Charter continued to be circulated secretly and studied by activists. Its demand for a democratic, non-racial South Africa — with nationalisation of mines and banks, free education and equal rights regardless of race — defined the ANC’s programme. When the UDF was formed in 1983, it explicitly adopted the Freedom Charter as its guiding document, showing how the 1955 text remained alive through decades of repression.

The distinction between the ANC and the PAC remained significant throughout the 1960s and beyond. The PAC rejected working with white South Africans and focused exclusively on African leadership; the ANC maintained its multiracial approach, incorporating Coloured, Indian and white members within its alliance. Robert Sobukwe, the PAC’s founder, was imprisoned under a special “Sobukwe clause” that allowed his continued detention beyond his original sentence — a legal measure Parliament passed specifically to keep him imprisoned without trial.

The Pondoland Revolt 1960–1961

Sharpeville was the most famous episode of March 1960, but it was not the only uprising that year. The Pondoland revolt in the Transkei homeland saw rural Africans rise against hut tax increases, Bantustan control measures and forced cattle culling. The revolt was suppressed by the army and police, but it showed that apartheid was generating resistance in rural as well as urban areas. The Pondoland revolt is often overshadowed by Sharpeville in historical accounts but is significant as evidence of the breadth of opposition to apartheid.

lessons.title: Rivonia Trial and the long silence

before.content_html:
The Rivonia Farm Raid

On 11 July 1963, South African security police raided Liliesleaf Farm at Rivonia, a suburb north of Johannesburg. The farm had been used as the ANC’s underground headquarters. Police arrested seventeen people and seized documents including plans for Operation Mayibuye, an outline plan for a nationwide guerrilla campaign. Nelson Mandela, already imprisoned since August 1962 for leaving the country without a passport, was added to the accused.

The trial that followed — formally known as “State v Nelson Mandela and others” — ran from October 1963 to June 1964. Eight men stood trial on charges of sabotage and conspiracy to violently overthrow the state. Percy Yutar led the prosecution, calling for the death penalty; the defence was led by Bram Fischer.

Key Fact

On 12 June 1964, eight defendants — including Nelson Mandela, Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki, Ahmed Kathrada, Raymond Mhlaba, Elias Motsoaledi, Andrew Mlangeni and Denis Goldberg — were sentenced to life imprisonment. They were sent to Robben Island (Goldberg to Pretoria, as a white prisoner).

“I Am Prepared to Die”

On 20 April 1964, Mandela delivered a statement from the dock that lasted over four hours. He acknowledged the ANC’s involvement in sabotage but explained that it was a last resort chosen after peaceful methods had failed. He outlined the ANC’s vision of a democratic, non-racial South Africa. He concluded by stating that he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free and democratic society — words that became one of the most famous statements of the entire anti-apartheid struggle.

Mandela did not fabricate his defence: he acknowledged that MK had carried out sabotage. His argument was that the apartheid government’s violence against its own citizens had made peaceful protest impossible. This is historically significant because it shows the ANC’s leaders were transparent about their methods while insisting on the moral justice of their cause.

Robben Island became a symbol of apartheid repression. Prisoners were forced to do hard labour in a limestone quarry, kept in small cells, denied newspapers and restricted to one letter and one visit every six months. Mandela was placed in “D Block” in a small cell. Yet the island also became an informal “university” — prisoners educated one another through discussion and secretly circulated texts.

The imprisonment of the ANC’s senior leadership effectively silenced the movement inside South Africa for over a decade. Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki and others remained imprisoned throughout the 1960s and 1970s. This “long silence” forced the movement to rebuild around new leadership — most significantly the Black Consciousness Movement that emerged in the late 1960s.

Consequences of the Trial

The Rivonia Trial achieved both sides’ aims — partially. The apartheid government removed the ANC’s top leadership from active politics for at least a generation. But the prosecution unwittingly created martyrs: Mandela’s dock statement was smuggled out and circulated internationally, boosting the ANC’s reputation abroad. The United Nations passed resolutions calling for the release of the Rivonia prisoners.

Key Fact

The Rivonia Trial removed the ANC’s leadership from inside South Africa for decades but simultaneously turned the accused into global martyrs. Mandela’s “I am prepared to die” statement became an iconic text of the liberation struggle, read and discussed internationally.

Mandela remained on the United States’ terrorist watchlist until 2008 — long after the end of apartheid and his presidency of South Africa. This historical fact is a useful illustration of how “terrorism” as a label is politically applied: what one government calls terrorism, another calls legitimate armed resistance. The apartheid government’s designation of MK as a terrorist organisation was a political claim, not a neutral historical judgement.

The Underground ANC and the Continuation of Resistance

The conviction of the Rivonia defendants did not end all resistance inside South Africa. A small underground ANC network continued to operate, though it was severely weakened. Bram Fischer, after successfully defending the Rivonia accused, went underground himself. He was arrested in 1965, convicted under the Suppression of Communism Act, and died in prison in 1975.

The ANC on Robben Island also adapted: prisoners organised study circles, shared knowledge and debated political strategy. The island prison became, in the words of many who survived it, a “university.” Mandela studied Afrikaans, arguing that understanding the language and culture of the oppressor was necessary for the eventual negotiation he believed would come. This strategic patience — the long view — shaped how Mandela approached negotiations when they finally began in the 1980s.

International Solidarity and the ANC’s External Networks

From his Lusaka base, Oliver Tambo built alliances with the Soviet Union, Sweden, the Netherlands and other sympathetic governments, securing funding and logistical support for MK training camps. The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) recognised the ANC as the legitimate representative of the South African people. This international recognition was crucial — it meant that when the ANC returned to negotiations in the late 1980s, it came as a recognised political actor with decades of international legitimacy, not merely as a banned underground organisation.

lessons.title: Black Consciousness, Durban strikes and trade unions

before.content_html:
A New Philosophy of Liberation

After the Rivonia convictions and the “long silence” of the mid-1960s, resistance inside South Africa looked fragmented. It was in this context that a new philosophy emerged: Black Consciousness. Its central idea was that apartheid’s deepest damage was psychological — it had made black South Africans internalise a sense of inferiority. Before political liberation could happen, mental liberation must come first.

Steve Biko was the movement’s defining intellectual. Born in 1946 in King William’s Town, he became politically active while studying medicine at the University of Natal. He was a brilliant writer and speaker who argued, in plain language, that black people had to reject the white liberal view that integration with white society was the goal, and instead build pride, solidarity and culture on their own terms.

Key Fact

The South African Students’ Organisation (SASO) was founded in 1969, separating black students from white-liberal-dominated student organisations. Its founding argument was that black students must organise independently to build consciousness and self-reliance.

SASO and the Black People’s Convention

SASO spread rapidly through the black universities created by the Bantu Education system — in an irony of history, the very institutions designed to restrict black education became hotbeds of political organising. In 1972, the Black People’s Convention (BPC) was founded to carry Black Consciousness beyond the campuses into community organisations, sports clubs and cultural groups.

Mamphela Ramphele was among the key figures in the BCM. Women’s groups linked to the BCM organised welfare, health clinics and community centres in townships, showing that Black Consciousness was as much about building community capacity as about political protest.

Between January and March 1973, a wave of strikes swept through Durban involving approximately 100,000 workers in docks, factories, transport and municipal services. The Durban strikes were significant for several reasons. First, they demonstrated that black workers could organise collectively despite the apartheid government’s ban on black trade union membership. Second, they forced employers and the government to acknowledge that low wages and the pass system were economically as well as politically unsustainable.

The Durban strikes were largely peaceful. Workers walked out, demanded higher wages and, in many cases, secured modest increases. They were not led by a single organisation and were largely spontaneous — which made them harder for the government to suppress than a formal strike by a named union. They accelerated trade union organising: by the mid-1970s, embryonic independent black trade unions were emerging, which would become the basis for the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) founded in 1985.

Steve Biko’s Death in Custody

Steve Biko was banned (restricted from speaking publicly or meeting more than one person at a time) by the security police from 1973. On 18 August 1977, he was arrested at a police roadblock near Grahamstown. During interrogation at Port Elizabeth security police headquarters, he sustained severe brain injuries. He was transported 1,200 kilometres to Pretoria, naked and unconscious, in the back of a Land Rover. He died in a Pretoria prison on 12 September 1977.

An inquest court initially found no one criminally responsible for his death; the inquest was reopened in 1997 and found that members of the security police had caused his fatal injuries. The apartheid government at the time claimed he had died from a hunger strike, a claim that was false and was exposed by the inquest evidence. Biko’s death provoked international outrage. In October 1977, the government banned all the main BCM organisations.

Key Fact

Steve Biko died in police custody on 12 September 1977, from brain injuries sustained during interrogation. The government banned all major Black Consciousness organisations the following month. Biko’s death became one of the most powerful symbols of apartheid brutality.

Black Consciousness filled the organisational vacuum left by the Rivonia imprisonments. It helped shape the generation of students who would lead the Soweto uprising of 1976. Its emphasis on cultural pride and psychological liberation influenced how South Africans of all generations understood their struggle. However, the BCM did not form a conventional political party and its relationship with the ANC in exile was sometimes tense — the ANC’s multiracial philosophy differed from the BCM’s emphasis on black self-organisation.

before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the Soweto Uprising, make sure to distinguish between the immediate trigger (Afrikaans decree) and the deeper causes (Bantu Education, Black Consciousness, years of accumulated grievances). Examiners reward answers that show this distinction. Also be precise about the consequences: the death of Biko in September 1977 and the banning of BCM organisations in October 1977 are consequences connected to 1976, not separate events.
before.content_html:
The Trigger — Afrikaans Medium Decree

The immediate cause of the Soweto Uprising was an education policy. In 1974, the apartheid government issued the Afrikaans Medium Decree, requiring that half of all subjects in black secondary schools be taught in Afrikaans. Students and teachers resisted. Many teachers refused to teach in Afrikaans; students found it impossible to follow lessons in a language they did not know well. By 1976 the decree was being enforced — and resistance had been building for two years.

Students saw the decree as more than a language policy. Afrikaans was the language of the Afrikaner government and of apartheid itself. Being forced to learn in Afrikaans felt, to many students, like being forced to use the language of their oppressor. Black Consciousness ideas about pride and self-determination gave students the language and confidence to act.

Key Fact

On 16 June 1976, approximately 20,000 students marched in Soweto to protest the Afrikaans decree. Police opened fire on the crowd. Hector Pieterson, aged 12, was among the first killed. Sam Nzima’s photograph of a classmate carrying his body became the defining image of the uprising.

The Uprising Spreads

What began on 16 June 1976 as a student march became a nationwide wave of protest. By the end of 1977, somewhere between 600 and 700 people had been killed in protest-related violence across South Africa (estimates vary between state and human rights sources). Schools were burned, government buildings attacked and police stations stoned. The protests spread from Soweto to Cape Town, Port Elizabeth, Durban and many smaller townships.

Tsietsi Mashinini was the student leader who organised the initial march. After the uprising he fled South Africa. Thousands of young people followed — many of them crossing the border to join MK training camps in Angola and Tanzania. The generation of 1976 would become the foot soldiers of the anti-apartheid movement through the 1980s.

The apartheid government’s immediate response was to send police and later the army into townships. Tear gas, rubber bullets and live ammunition were used against protesters. Hundreds were arrested and detained without trial. In September 1977, Steve Biko died in police custody. The following month, October 1977, the government banned eighteen Black Consciousness organisations including SASO and the BPC. The message was clear: the regime intended to destroy the BCM as it had destroyed the ANC fifteen years earlier.

However, repression did not restore calm. International condemnation intensified. The United Nations Security Council passed a mandatory arms embargo against South Africa in November 1977 — a direct consequence of the Biko killing and the Soweto uprising. The regime found itself increasingly isolated.

The ANC in Exile and the Soweto Generation

The Soweto uprising reinvigorated the ANC’s external mission. Oliver Tambo in Lusaka greeted the young people streaming out of South Africa. MK training camps absorbed thousands of new recruits. At the same time, the uprising showed the ANC’s exile leadership that resistance inside South Africa was alive and self-generating — it did not depend solely on direction from Lusaka. The “internal” and “external” wings of the movement were reconnecting.

Key Fact

The Soweto uprising had two major long-term consequences: (1) it produced a new generation of activists — many joining MK — who would drive the anti-apartheid struggle through the 1980s; and (2) the global outrage it generated accelerated the international isolation of apartheid South Africa.

In post-apartheid South Africa, 16 June is commemorated as Youth Day — a national holiday marking the 1976 uprising. Hector Pieterson’s name is given to a memorial and museum in Soweto. This shows how significant the uprising has been judged to be by those who lived through it and inherited its legacy: it is treated as a founding moment of the new South Africa, not merely as a historical episode.

The International Dimension — Footage That Changed Minds

The Soweto uprising unfolded in front of international cameras and wire-service photographers. Sam Nzima’s photograph of Hector Pieterson was published around the world within days. Television footage of police chasing schoolchildren through the streets of Soweto reached audiences in Europe and North America who had known little about apartheid’s day-to-day reality. The visual power of the uprising transformed the AAM’s recruitment capacity in the UK, Australia and the United States — organisations that had struggled to interest the public now had queues of volunteers.

The apartheid government attempted to minimise and misrepresent the scale of the uprising. Official statements initially blamed “outside agitators” and “communists,” a framing that convinced few international observers. The state’s credibility had already been damaged by the Biko killing; combined with the Soweto images, the international community’s patience with constructive engagement arguments was wearing thin. The UN mandatory arms embargo of November 1977 was a direct consequence.

Education and Resistance — A Deeper Connection

The Soweto uprising was not simply a spontaneous reaction to the Afrikaans decree. Students were organised: the Soweto Students’ Representative Council had been active before June 1976. Black Consciousness ideas had been circulating in Soweto’s schools for several years. The BCM’s message that black South Africans must assert their own dignity and refuse to accept inferior status gave students a framework for action that went far beyond language policy. In this sense, the uprising was the product of years of organising — the Afrikaans decree was the trigger, not the cause.

lessons.title: International isolation and the Anti-Apartheid Movement

before.content_html:
The International Response to Apartheid

Resistance to apartheid was not confined to South Africa. From the early 1960s, an international movement grew to isolate the apartheid regime through boycotts, sanctions and public protest. The Anti-Apartheid Movement (AAM) was founded in Britain in 1959, initially as a small activist group. By the 1980s it had become a mass movement with significant political influence.

Trevor Huddleston, an Anglican priest who had lived and worked in Sophiatown (a vibrant mixed-race area of Johannesburg that was demolished under the Group Areas Act), was a founding figure of the British AAM. His memoir Naught for Your Comfort (1956) had introduced many British readers to the reality of apartheid.

Key Fact

Three major forms of international pressure combined: sports isolation (South Africa excluded from the Olympics from 1964; Gleneagles Agreement 1977 on Commonwealth sports), economic sanctions (US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act 1986; Chase Manhattan refused to roll over loans 1985) and diplomatic isolation (expelled from the Commonwealth 1961; UN mandatory arms embargo 1977).

Sports Isolation

Sport was among the most publicly visible fronts of the isolation campaign. South Africa was excluded from the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and banned from all subsequent Games until 1992. In 1970 the International Cricket Conference expelled South Africa. The Gleneagles Agreement (1977) committed Commonwealth governments to discouraging sporting contact with South Africa. When rebel cricket and rugby tours were organised in defiance of the boycott, they provoked significant protests.

For many white South Africans, the sports boycott was among the most psychologically damaging forms of isolation — South Africa had strong sporting traditions and international competition mattered to white identity. Apartheid supporters argued the boycott was “politics in sport”; anti-apartheid campaigners replied that apartheid itself had already politicised sport by enforcing racial selection policies.

Economic pressure grew through the 1980s. In 1985, the Chase Manhattan Bank refused to roll over South Africa’s short-term loans — a dramatic signal that international financial confidence in the regime was collapsing. Other banks followed. The South African government declared a debt moratorium in September 1985.

In 1986, the United States Congress passed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act, imposing sweeping economic sanctions. President Reagan vetoed the bill on “constructive engagement” grounds, but Congress overrode his veto — a rare and significant act. Universities, pension funds and corporations across the US and Europe were pressured by campaign groups to divest from companies doing business in South Africa.

Oliver Tambo and Desmond Tutu

Oliver Tambo’s work in exile was central to the international campaign. He lobbied the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and sympathetic governments. The ANC under his leadership maintained MK training camps and built alliances with the Soviet Union, Sweden and other states that provided financial and logistical support.

Desmond Tutu, Archbishop of Cape Town from 1986 and Nobel Peace Prize winner (1984), was one of the most prominent internal voices calling for sanctions. He argued that economic pressure was the only non-violent alternative to escalating violence inside South Africa.

Key Fact

Reagan and Thatcher both opposed comprehensive sanctions, arguing that “constructive engagement” — maintaining economic ties — would encourage reform more effectively. Critics (including Tutu and the ANC) argued this was a justification for protecting Western economic interests and that it gave the regime legitimacy it did not deserve.

South Africa had been expelled from the Commonwealth in 1961. In 1977, following Biko’s death and the Soweto uprising, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 418 — a mandatory arms embargo that required all member states to stop selling weapons to South Africa. This was the UN’s most significant direct action against apartheid. South Africa responded by developing its own arms industry (Armscor) and seeking covert supplies, but the embargo nonetheless damaged its military capacity.

Corporate Disinvestment and the Campaign in Universities

Beyond government sanctions, the disinvestment campaign targeted private companies. Barclays Bank — which had a major presence in South Africa through its subsidiary Barclays National Bank — faced sustained protests in British universities during the late 1970s and early 1980s. Students union campaigns against Barclays culminated in the bank selling its South African subsidiary in 1986. Shell, IBM and dozens of other corporations came under similar pressure from shareholders and consumers to divest from South Africa. By 1987, over 200 American companies had withdrawn investments.

The Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group (EPG) visited South Africa in 1986 to explore whether conditions for negotiation existed. The EPG recommended comprehensive Commonwealth sanctions after the South African government launched military raids into Zambia, Zimbabwe and Botswana — frontline states supporting the ANC — during the very week the EPG was visiting. Only Thatcher’s Britain blocked full Commonwealth sanctions, but the political isolation was already overwhelming.

lessons.title: P.W. Botha's State of Emergency and total strategy

before.content_html:
A New Constitution and a New Opposition

P.W. Botha became Prime Minister in 1978 promising a “total strategy” — using military force, limited political reform and regional destabilisation to counter what he called the “total onslaught” of communist-backed resistance. His most significant constitutional change was the Tricameral Parliament introduced under the 1983 constitution, which created separate parliamentary chambers for Coloured and Indian voters — while leaving black South Africans with no representation at all.

The Tricameral Parliament provoked a powerful response. In August 1983, the United Democratic Front (UDF) was launched at a mass meeting in Cape Town. It brought together over 400 trade unions, church groups, civic organisations and student bodies under a single anti-apartheid umbrella. The UDF explicitly aligned itself with the ANC’s Freedom Charter.

Key Fact

The United Democratic Front (UDF) was founded in August 1983, uniting over 400 organisations. It brought the ANC’s internal network back to life despite the ANC being banned — the UDF acted as a legal front for anti-apartheid organising inside South Africa while the ANC remained banned.

Township Revolt 1984–1986

From late 1984, a mass uprising swept through South Africa’s black townships. Rent boycotts, school boycotts and strikes paralysed many areas. Black local councillors appointed under the tricameral system were attacked as collaborators — some were killed. Police and army units entered townships in armoured vehicles, making mass arrests. Funerals became political demonstrations, which the government tried to ban.

Key leaders of the UDF included Allan Boesak and Frank Chikane, both ministers of religion who used their standing in the churches to mobilise communities. The UDF explicitly advocated non-violence, though the scale of township violence during this period meant that the boundary between protest and armed conflict was often unclear.

Botha declared a partial State of Emergency in July 1985, extended to a national State of Emergency in June 1986. Under emergency powers, the security forces could detain people without charge, ban meetings and restrict reporting. At its peak, an estimated 30,000 people were detained. Censorship made it difficult for journalists to report the extent of the violence.

The State of Emergency temporarily suppressed the most visible protests but did not restore political stability. The economic consequences of continued unrest — combined with the Chase Manhattan Bank crisis of August 1985 — made the regime’s position increasingly precarious.

Inkatha and the Violence in KwaZulu-Natal

Inkatha, the Zulu cultural movement led by Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, was a significant and complex force in 1980s South Africa. Inkatha opposed sanctions and the ANC’s armed struggle, and clashed violently with UDF and ANC-aligned organisations, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal.

The third force — the use of covert state agents to arm and fund Inkatha against the ANC — was documented in detail by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The TRC found that the security forces had supplied weapons to Inkatha and had carried out “black-on-black” violence to discredit the ANC. These are the TRC’s findings; the apartheid government denied any such programme at the time.

Key Fact

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (established 1995) documented that apartheid security forces had covertly armed Inkatha to use against the ANC in a “third force” programme. The TRC heard testimony from security operatives who admitted their role. This means the Inkatha-ANC violence of the 1980s was not simply ethnic conflict — it was partly orchestrated by the state.

In August 1985, P.W. Botha was widely expected to announce major reforms in a speech. International markets and foreign banks waited. Instead, Botha delivered a defiant speech refusing any fundamental change — this became known as the “Rubicon speech.” It confirmed for international investors that the regime had no credible reform plan, contributing directly to the Chase Manhattan Bank crisis days later. Botha’s failure to cross his own metaphorical Rubicon accelerated the regime’s financial crisis.

MK Activity Inside South Africa — The Return

The 1980s also saw an intensification of MK operations inside South Africa. After a period of relative quiet following the Rivonia imprisonments, MK’s sabotage campaign resumed with greater frequency. Notable operations included the 1980 attack on the SASOL oil refinery and the 1983 Church Street bombing in Pretoria which killed 19 people and injured over 200. The Church Street bombing was controversial even within the anti-apartheid movement: it targeted a military building but killed civilians too. The ANC acknowledged that MK operations evolved beyond purely infrastructure sabotage during this period.

The TRC process (1995–2002) examined MK’s operations alongside state atrocities. The TRC found that the ANC had committed human rights abuses — including through “necklacing” (burning alleged informers with petrol-soaked tyres in townships) carried out by ANC-aligned groups, and through abuses in MK exile camps. These findings are documented by the TRC and must be stated accurately: the ANC was not solely a victim in the conflict. However, the TRC also found that the apartheid state’s abuses were far more systematic and numerous than those of any non-state actor.
before.exam_tip_html: The UDF and State of Emergency are often paired in exam questions. Be precise: the UDF was legal (it was not banned until 1988), and it operated as an internal network aligned with the banned ANC. When discussing the State of Emergency, give specific evidence (dates, detention numbers) rather than vague references to “repression.” The Inkatha-ANC violence is also examiner material — be prepared to explain why this was not simply ethnic conflict.

lessons.title: Cuito Cuanavale, de Klerk and the negotiation begins

before.content_html:
South Africa’s War in Angola

From the mid-1970s, South Africa’s Defence Force (SADF) was involved in the Angolan civil war, supporting UNITA rebels against the MPLA government (which was backed by Cuba and the Soviet Union). The apartheid government justified this as part of its “total strategy” to prevent a communist-aligned state on its border. MK maintained training camps in Angola, making the conflict directly connected to the anti-apartheid struggle.

In 1987–88, the largest conventional battles in Africa since the Second World War were fought around the town of Cuito Cuanavale. Cuban forces had deployed in large numbers to reinforce the Angolan army. The outcome was militarily disputed — the SADF prevented the fall of UNITA positions, but Cuban and Angolan forces prevented a decisive SADF victory, and the SADF took significant casualties.

Key Fact

Both sides claimed victory at Cuito Cuanavale. South African sources emphasised that UNITA positions held; Cuban and ANC sources emphasised that the SADF’s advance was stopped and it eventually withdrew. Historians including Stephen Ellis and Piero Gleijeses have offered different assessments. What is clear is that South Africa subsequently agreed to the Tripartite Accord of December 1988, withdrawing from Angola and Namibia.

Divisions Within the National Party

By 1989, P.W. Botha had suffered a stroke and was increasingly isolated within his own party. His refusal to negotiate fundamentally with the ANC was seen by a growing faction within the NP as politically and economically unsustainable. In August 1989, F.W. de Klerk replaced Botha as State President. De Klerk represented a pragmatic wing of the NP that recognised the regime could not survive indefinitely.

De Klerk was not an opponent of apartheid — he had been a loyal NP minister for years. But he understood that the combination of economic crisis, international isolation, internal unrest and the failure of “total strategy” in Angola had left the regime with no viable path forward except negotiation. His decision to go further than any of his predecessors was a calculation of survival, not a conversion to liberalism.

On 2 February 1990, de Klerk delivered a landmark speech to parliament in which he announced the unbanning of the ANC, PAC and South African Communist Party (SACP), the suspension of capital punishment, and the planned release of Nelson Mandela. The speech shocked both supporters and opponents. On 11 February 1990, Mandela walked free from Victor Verster Prison after 27 years of imprisonment.

Mandela’s release was broadcast live around the world. His first public address in Cape Town drew a vast crowd. He affirmed the ANC’s commitment to negotiation but also to the continuation of the armed struggle — MK’s weapons would not be surrendered until a new democratic constitution was in place. This position caused tension with the government but was consistent with the ANC’s negotiating position throughout.

CODESA and the Path to Agreement

In December 1991, negotiations began under the banner CODESA (Convention for a Democratic South Africa). The ANC’s chief negotiator was Cyril Ramaphosa; the government’s was Roelf Meyer. The negotiations were complicated by continuing political violence: in June 1992, the Boipatong massacre killed 45 people and the ANC temporarily withdrew from talks.

In April 1993, the assassination of Chris Hani, leader of the South African Communist Party and a popular ANC figure, by a right-wing Polish immigrant nearly collapsed the entire process. It was Mandela who addressed the nation on television, calling for calm — not de Klerk — demonstrating the degree to which Mandela’s moral authority had surpassed the State President’s.

Key Fact

CODESA produced the Interim Constitution, agreed in November 1993, which set the framework for the April 1994 elections. Despite the Boipatong massacre (June 1992) and the assassination of Chris Hani (April 1993), both of which temporarily halted talks, the negotiations ultimately succeeded.

De Klerk has argued in his memoirs that his decision was motivated by moral conviction as well as pragmatism. Historians are divided: some, like F. van Zyl Slabbert, emphasise the regime’s impossible economic and political position; others give more weight to de Klerk’s personal decision-making. For exam purposes, it is important to present both de Klerk’s stated rationale (principled recognition that apartheid was morally wrong and politically exhausted) and the structural pressures (economic crisis, Angola failure, international isolation) that shaped his choice.

Convention for a Democratic South Africa — the formal multi-party negotiation forum launched in December 1991 to agree a new constitutional framework.
ANC negotiator who led the multi-party talks at CODESA; later South Africa's first post-apartheid Deputy President and subsequent President.
National Party negotiator at CODESA who developed a close working relationship with Cyril Ramaphosa.
A massacre in which 45 residents of the Vaal township of Boipatong were killed in June 1992; the ANC alleged security force complicity and temporarily withdrew from talks.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the CODESA negotiations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names CODESA AND gives a precise feature, e.g. the ANC's chief negotiator was Cyril Ramaphosa and the government's was Roelf Meyer; or CODESA produced an Interim Constitution agreed in November 1993. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to negotiations. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of F.W. de Klerk's speech of 2 February 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two precise features — e.g. (1) he announced the unbanning of the ANC, PAC and SACP; (2) he announced the planned release of Nelson Mandela. Secure: Two features identified, one with clear detail. Developing: Two features with limited detail. Emerging: One feature or very general response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why F.W. de Klerk decided to unban the ANC and enter negotiations in 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the combination of economic crisis (Chase Manhattan, sanctions) and internal unrest had left the regime in an unsustainable position; (2) the failure of 'total strategy' in Angola (Cuito Cuanavale, Tripartite Accord) had undermined military confidence. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the negotiations between the ANC and the apartheid government were nearly derailed in 1992–1993.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the Boipatong massacre (June 1992) killed 45 people and the ANC alleged security force complicity, withdrawing from talks; (2) the assassination of Chris Hani (April 1993) provoked mass anger that threatened violent breakdown. Secure: Two reasons with good detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of the Battle of Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88) for the apartheid regime.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more points — contested military outcome; SADF took casualties; led to Tripartite Accord and withdrawal from Angola and Namibia; undermined regime's claim that 'total strategy' could contain resistance; heightened divisions within NP. Secure: Two or three points with detail. Developing: One or two points. Emerging: Very general response.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the role of F.W. de Klerk in bringing apartheid to an end? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing de Klerk's significance (unbanning, Mandela release, CODESA leadership) against the structural factors that made change inevitable (economic crisis, Angola failure, sanctions, internal unrest, ANC negotiating position under Mandela and Ramaphosa); reaches a supported judgement about 'how significant'. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of de Klerk's actions with limited analysis of wider factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

lessons.title: Election 1994 and the new South Africa

before.content_html:
South Africa’s First Non-Racial Election

On 27–29 April 1994, South Africa held its first non-racial general election. Voters of all races could vote for the first time. The proportional representation system meant that parties won seats broadly in line with their share of the vote. The turnout was enormous: an estimated 19.7 million people voted out of a total eligible electorate of about 22 million.

Images of queues stretching for kilometres became iconic around the world — many people waiting for hours, some for an entire day, to cast their first vote. For millions who had never voted, the act of placing a ballot was itself a historic and emotional experience. International observers, including former US President Jimmy Carter and teams from the United Nations and the Commonwealth, declared the election substantially free and fair.

Key Fact

The ANC won 62.6 per cent of the vote — a large majority but just below the two-thirds required to rewrite the constitution unilaterally. The NP won 20.4 per cent; the Inkatha Freedom Party won 10.5 per cent, predominantly in KwaZulu-Natal. The results broadly followed racial voting patterns but Mandela won respect across racial lines.

The Government of National Unity

The negotiated settlement had included a “sunset clause” — agreed by the ANC’s negotiators — requiring the formation of a Government of National Unity (GNU) for five years. Under this arrangement, any party winning more than 20 per cent of the vote was entitled to cabinet representation. F.W. de Klerk became one of two Deputy Presidents alongside Thabo Mbeki.

The sunset clause was controversial within the ANC. Some felt it gave too much to the NP and left key state structures — including the civil service, the security forces and the judiciary — largely unchanged. Joe Slovo, the SACP leader who proposed the sunset clauses, argued it was the price of a peaceful transition. Historians continue to debate whether the compromise was a triumph of pragmatism or a structural limit on transformation.

On 9 May 1994, the new National Assembly elected Nelson Mandela as President. His inauguration on 10 May 1994, at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, was attended by world leaders and broadcast globally. South African Air Force jets flew overhead — the same force that had been used to enforce apartheid now saluting a black president.

Mandela’s inauguration speech emphasised reconciliation. He spoke of “a rainbow nation at peace with itself and the world” — a phrase that captured the mood of the moment. Archbishop Desmond Tutu’s phrase “rainbow nation” entered global consciousness. However, historians note that the euphoria of 1994 should be distinguished from the realities that followed — poverty, inequality and land distribution remained largely unresolved.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission

In 1995, the new South African parliament established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. The TRC invited perpetrators of human rights violations to apply for amnesty in exchange for full and honest disclosure of their crimes. Victims were able to tell their stories publicly.

The TRC documented atrocities committed by ALL sides — the apartheid state, the ANC and MK, Inkatha and the “third force.” The ANC was found to have committed human rights abuses in its exile camps; MK had used violence that harmed civilians in some operations; the state’s atrocities were the most systematic and the most numerous. The TRC’s approach was deliberately neither amnesty without accountability nor criminal prosecution without acknowledgement — it was a compromise designed for a society that needed to function together.

Key Fact

The 1996 Final Constitution, adopted two years after the election, replaced the Interim Constitution and enshrined a bill of rights, independent judiciary and constitutional democracy. South Africa’s transformation was legal and constitutional, but structural inequalities — land, wealth, access to education — inherited from apartheid proved much harder to address.

The 1994 election ended formal apartheid and established a constitutional democracy. It did not redistribute land or wealth. The “sunset clauses” left existing state employees — including apartheid-era security officials — in post. No significant land reform occurred; South Africa remained one of the most unequal societies on earth. These realities were known at the time — the ANC accepted them as the price of a peaceful transition, a choice that remained contested among its supporters.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Government of National Unity formed after the 1994 election.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the GNU AND gives a precise feature, e.g. parties winning over 20 per cent of the vote were entitled to cabinet representation; or F.W. de Klerk became one of two Deputy Presidents. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to a coalition government. Emerging: Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two precise features — e.g. (1) it offered amnesty in exchange for full and honest disclosure of human rights abuses; (2) it documented atrocities by all sides, including the ANC and MK as well as the apartheid state. Secure: Two features identified, one with clear detail. Developing: Two features with limited detail. Emerging: One feature or very general response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the 1994 election result was considered significant both inside and outside South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) it was the first non-racial election, giving millions of black South Africans a vote for the first time — itself a historic achievement; (2) it produced a large ANC majority that gave Mandela a democratic mandate to lead reconstruction; (3) the international community (UN, Commonwealth observers) validated the process as free and fair. Each reason with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two limitations of the changes brought about by the 1994 election in South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the sunset clauses left apartheid-era civil servants and security officials in post, preventing restructuring of the state; (2) no significant land redistribution occurred, leaving South Africa one of the most unequal societies on earth. Secure: Two reasons with good detail. Developing: One well-explained reason. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main events of South Africa's 1994 election and its immediate aftermath.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more events with detail — 27–29 April election; ANC wins 62.6%; Mandela elected by National Assembly 9 May; inauguration 10 May; GNU formed; TRC established 1995; Final Constitution 1996. Secure: Two or three events with detail. Developing: One or two events. Emerging: Very general response.

practice_questions.text: How far did the end of apartheid in 1994 represent a complete transformation of South African society? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing what changed (formal apartheid ended, non-racial democracy established, Mandela as president, TRC process) against what remained the same (land distribution, economic inequality, sunset clauses preserving state structures); reaches a supported judgement on 'how far'. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of 1994 with limited analysis of structural continuities. Emerging: Narrative description.

before.exam_tip_html: Questions about the 1994 election often ask you to assess its significance. Be balanced: the election was genuinely historic — the end of formal apartheid, Mandela as president, the TRC process. But examiners also credit answers that note what was NOT achieved: land redistribution, economic equality, fundamental restructuring of the state. The “sunset clause” compromise is a good example of a complex outcome to discuss.
